whyNext: Builds on two-pointer symmetry checking from Valid Palindrome (Seq 22) by swapping characters between converging left and right pointers to reverse an array in-place.
hints: Use two pointers starting at the opposite ends of the character array.
Swap the elements at the pointers and move them toward the center until they meet.
Initialize left = 0, right = s.length - 1. While left < right, swap s[left] and s[right], then increment left and decrement right.

brute.idea: Create an auxiliary array of the same length, copy elements in reverse order, and write back.
steps: Allocate a new character array copy of size s.length.
Loop i from 0 to s.length - 1: copy[i] = s[s.length - 1 - i].
Copy elements from copy back into s.
Finish with reversed s in place.
brute.whySlow: Allocates O(n) auxiliary memory instead of swapping elements directly in-place.

optimal.idea: Converging two pointers swapping elements in-place with O(1) auxiliary space.
steps: Initialize left = 0 and right = s.length - 1.
While left < right: swap s[left] and s[right].
Increment left and decrement right.
Termination occurs when pointers cross at the center.

whyNext: Builds on two-pointer in-place reversal from Reverse String (Seq 329) by advancing pointers conditionally to only swap vowels while leaving consonants in their original positions.
hints: Use two pointers, but only swap when both pointers are positioned at vowel characters.
Check if each character is in the set of vowels ('a', 'e', 'i', 'o', 'u', case-insensitive); skip non-vowels.
Initialize left = 0, right = s.length - 1. While left < right: increment left while s[left] is not a vowel; decrement right while s[right] is not a vowel; swap if left < right; advance both.

brute.idea: Collect all vowels into a list, reverse the list, and replace vowels in the string in a second pass.
steps: Iterate through s and collect all vowel characters into a list.
Reverse the vowels list.
Iterate through s again; whenever a vowel is encountered, replace it with the next vowel from the list.
Return the reconstructed string.
brute.whySlow: Requires two passes and O(n) auxiliary storage for the collected vowel list.

optimal.idea: Two-pointer approach converging from both ends, advancing past non-vowels and swapping vowels in-place.
steps: Convert string to a char array.
Initialize left = 0 and right = arr.length - 1.
While left < right: advance left while left < right and arr[left] is not vowel.
Advance right while left < right and arr[right] is not vowel.
Swap arr[left] and arr[right], then increment left and decrement right.
Convert char array back to String and return.

whyNext: Builds on in-place array modification from Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array (Seq 30) by maintaining a write pointer that retains only values not matching val.
hints: Use a slow pointer for the write index and a fast pointer to inspect each element.
Whenever the current element is not equal to val, copy it to the write index and advance the write index.
Initialize k = 0. Iterate i through nums; if nums[i] != val, set nums[k] = nums[i] and increment k. Return k.

brute.idea: Whenever val is encountered, shift all subsequent elements to the left by one position.
steps: Let n = nums.length.
Iterate i from 0 to n - 1.
If nums[i] == val, shift elements from i + 1 to n - 1 left by 1, decrement n and decrement i.
Return n as the new length.
brute.whySlow: Shifting elements for every occurrence of val takes O(n²) worst-case time.

optimal.idea: Fast and slow pointer: copy elements not equal to val to the slow write pointer in O(n) time.
steps: Initialize write pointer k = 0.
Iterate read pointer i from 0 to nums.length - 1.
If nums[i] != val, assign nums[k] = nums[i] and increment k.
Return k as the count of elements remaining.

whyNext: Builds on merging two sorted sequences from Merge Two Sorted Lists (Seq 84) by merging backwards from the end of nums1 to avoid overwriting unread elements.
hints: Instead of inserting from the front which requires shifting, insert the largest elements from the back.
Compare nums1[p1] and nums2[p2], placing the larger value at index p = m + n - 1.
Initialize p1 = m - 1, p2 = n - 1, p = m + n - 1. While p2 >= 0: if p1 >= 0 and nums1[p1] > nums2[p2], nums1[p--] = nums1[p1--]; else nums1[p--] = nums2[p2--].

brute.idea: Copy elements of nums2 into the end of nums1 and sort the entire combined array.
steps: Copy elements from nums2 into nums1 starting at index m.
Call Arrays.sort(nums1) or sort(nums1) on the combined array.
nums1 is now fully sorted.
brute.whySlow: Sorting an array that is already mostly sorted takes O((m + n) log(m + n)) time.

optimal.idea: Three pointers starting from the ends of nums1 and nums2, filling nums1 backwards from index m + n - 1 in O(m + n) time.
steps: Initialize p1 = m - 1, p2 = n - 1, and p = m + n - 1.
While p2 >= 0: if p1 >= 0 and nums1[p1] > nums2[p2], place nums1[p--] = nums1[p1--].
Else place nums1[p--] = nums2[p2--].
All elements are merged in sorted order in-place.

whyNext: Builds on two-pointer reading from Remove Element (Seq 331) by advancing a source pointer whenever a character in the target string matches the current sequence character.
hints: Iterate through string t and advance a pointer in s whenever characters match.
If the pointer in s reaches s.length(), then all characters of s appeared in order within t.
Initialize i = 0, j = 0. While i < s.length() and j < t.length(): if s[i] == t[j], increment i. In all cases, increment j. Return i == s.length().

brute.idea: Generate all subsequences of string t and check if string s is among them.
steps: Generate all 2^len(t) subsequences of string t.
Check if s exists in the generated set of subsequences.
Return true if found, false otherwise.
brute.whySlow: Generating all subsequences takes exponential O(2^len(t)) time.

optimal.idea: Two pointers scanning greedily: advance pattern pointer i on match, always advance text pointer j.
steps: Initialize i = 0 and j = 0.
While i < s.length() and j < t.length(): if s.charAt(i) == t.charAt(j), increment i.
Increment j regardless.
Return i == s.length().

whyNext: Builds on Two Sum II (Seq 24) two-pointer pair searching by sorting the array and pairing smallest and largest elements that sum to k, removing paired elements.
hints: Sorting the array allows two pointers from opposite ends to find pairs that sum to k.
If nums[left] + nums[right] == k, increment count, advance left, and decrement right.
Sort nums. Initialize l = 0, r = nums.length - 1, count = 0. While l < r: sum = nums[l] + nums[r]. If sum == k: count++, l++, r--; else if sum < k: l++; else r--. Return count.

brute.idea: Use a boolean array to mark used elements and find pairs summing to k with nested loops.
steps: Create boolean visited array of size n.
Iterate i from 0 to n - 1.
If visited[i] is true, continue.
Search j from i + 1 to n - 1: if !visited[j] and nums[i] + nums[j] == k, mark visited[i] and visited[j], increment count, and break.
Return count.
brute.whySlow: Nested loop pair searching with visited tracking takes O(n²) time.

optimal.idea: Sort the array and use two pointers converging from both ends to match pairs summing to k in O(n log n) time.
steps: Sort nums in ascending order.
Initialize l = 0, r = nums.length - 1, ops = 0.
While l < r: calculate sum = nums[l] + nums[r].
If sum == k: increment ops, l++, r--.
Else if sum < k: increment l.
Else: decrement r.
Return ops.

whyNext: Builds on two-pointer pair matching from Max Number of K-Sum Pairs (Seq 334) by pairing the heaviest and lightest individuals under a boat capacity limit.
hints: Greedily pair the heaviest person with the lightest person if their combined weight fits in the boat.
If the heaviest person cannot share a boat with the lightest person, they must take a boat alone.
Sort people. Set l = 0, r = people.length - 1, boats = 0. While l <= r: if people[l] + people[r] <= limit, l++; r--; boats++; return boats.

brute.idea: Try all combinations of pairing people together using backtracking to find minimum boats.
steps: Sort people array.
Try putting pairs together or single individuals in boats recursively.
Track minimum boat count across all valid assignments.
Return the minimal count.
brute.whySlow: Backtracking all partitionings takes exponential time O(2ⁿ).

optimal.idea: Sort people and greedily pair the heaviest with lightest using two pointers in O(n log n) time.
steps: Sort people in ascending order.
Initialize l = 0, r = people.length - 1, boats = 0.
While l <= r: if people[l] + people[r] <= limit, l++ (lightest joins).
Decrement r (heaviest always boards a boat).
Increment boats counter.
Return boats.

whyNext: Builds on Two Sum II (Seq 24) two-pointer search by testing integer candidate squares a² + b² = c with pointers running from 0 and floor(sqrt(c)).
hints: The value of a can start at 0, and the value of b can start at integer floor of sqrt(c).
Calculate a * a + b * b; if sum == c, return true; if sum < c, increment a; if sum > c, decrement b.
Initialize a = 0, b = (long) Math.sqrt(c). While a <= b: val = a*a + b*b. If val == c return true; else if val < c a++; else b--. Return false.

brute.idea: Iterate all candidate integers a from 0 up to sqrt(c) and check if c - a² is a perfect square.
steps: Loop a from 0 up to sqrt(c).
Let rem = c - a * a.
Compute b = round(sqrt(rem)).
If b * b == rem, return true.
Return false if loop terminates without finding a match.
brute.whySlow: Square root computations inside the loop incur repeated floating point overhead.

optimal.idea: Two pointers converging from 0 and floor(sqrt(c)) using 64-bit integer arithmetic to prevent overflow.
steps: Initialize left = 0 and right = (long) Math.sqrt(c).
While left <= right: calculate sum = left * left + right * right.
If sum == c, return true.
If sum < c, increment left.
If sum > c, decrement right.
Return false if pointers cross.

whyNext: Builds on running window evaluation from Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (Seq 37) by maintaining a fixed-size sliding window of length k and tracking vowel count updates.
hints: Instead of recounting vowels for every window of size k, adjust the count when sliding.
Add 1 if the incoming character is a vowel, and subtract 1 if the outgoing character was a vowel.
Compute vowel count in first k chars. Then loop i from k to s.length(): if s[i] is vowel count++, if s[i-k] is vowel count--, maxVowels = max(maxVowels, count). Return maxVowels.

brute.idea: Inspect every possible substring of length k and count its vowels linearly.
steps: Iterate i from 0 to s.length() - k.
Count the vowels in substring s.substring(i, i + k).
Update maxCount with the highest count found.
Return maxCount.
brute.whySlow: Counting vowels in every k-length substring takes O(n * k) time.

optimal.idea: Sliding window of fixed size k updating vowel count in O(1) time per step.
steps: Count vowels in the initial window s[0..k-1] to set currentCount.
Set maxCount = currentCount.
For i from k to s.length() - 1: if s[i] is vowel, currentCount++; if s[i - k] is vowel, currentCount--.
Update maxCount = max(maxCount, currentCount).
Return maxCount.

whyNext: Inverts fixed-size sliding window logic from Maximum Number of Vowels (Seq 337) by minimizing the sum of an unpicked contiguous window of size n - k to maximize the picked card endpoints.
hints: Taking k cards from the ends is equivalent to leaving behind a contiguous subarray of length n - k.
To maximize the sum of cards taken, minimize the sum of the remaining subarray of length n - k.
Calculate totalSum. Let windowSize = n - k. Find minimum subarray sum of size windowSize using sliding window. Return totalSum - minSubarraySum.

brute.idea: Compute all k + 1 combinations of taking i cards from the left and (k - i) cards from the right.
steps: Let n = cardPoints.length.
For i from 0 to k: sum i elements from front and (k - i) elements from back.
Track the maximum sum over all choices of i.
Return the maximum sum.
brute.whySlow: Summing left and right slices for each i takes O(k²) time.

optimal.idea: Sliding window of size n - k to find the minimum sum subarray left behind, maximizing card score.
steps: Let n = cardPoints.length, windowSize = n - k.
Compute totalSum of all elements.
If windowSize == 0, return totalSum.
Compute initial windowSum of first windowSize elements.
Slide window across array, updating minWindowSum = min(minWindowSum, windowSum).
Return totalSum - minWindowSum.

whyNext: Adapts flexible sliding window from Max Consecutive Ones III (Seq 45) specifically bounded to at most one zero deletion, measuring the longest resulting span minus one.
hints: Find the longest subarray containing at most one zero.
Use a sliding window with left and right pointers, expanding right and contracting left whenever zeroes > 1.
Initialize left = 0, zeroes = 0, maxLen = 0. Iterate right: if nums[right] == 0, zeroes++. While zeroes > 1: if nums[left] == 0 zeroes--, left++. maxLen = max(maxLen, right - left). Return maxLen.

brute.idea: Test every index i: simulate deleting nums[i] and count the maximum streak of ones.
steps: For each index i from 0 to n - 1: create a temporary array omitting nums[i].
Compute the longest consecutive sequence of 1s in the temporary array.
Track the maximum length across all choices of i.
Return the maximum length.
brute.whySlow: Simulating deletion for each of n indices takes O(n²) time.

optimal.idea: Sliding window allowing at most one zero: length of window minus one is the maximum consecutive ones.
steps: Initialize l = 0, zeroCount = 0, maxLen = 0.
Iterate r from 0 to nums.length - 1: if nums[r] == 0, increment zeroCount.
While zeroCount > 1: if nums[l] == 0, decrement zeroCount; increment l.
Update maxLen = max(maxLen, r - l).
Return maxLen.

whyNext: Combines unique element sliding window from Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (Seq 38) with running sum accumulation to maximize score over unique-element subarrays.
hints: Maintain a window with no duplicate elements while tracking the sum of elements currently in the window.
When a duplicate is encountered at the right edge, shrink the window from the left and subtract elements from running sum until unique.

Initialize left = 0, curSum = 0, maxSum = 0, and a HashSet. For right from 0 to n-1: while set contains nums[right], remove nums[left], curSum -= nums[left], left++. Add nums[right], curSum += nums[right], maxSum = max(maxSum, curSum).

brute.idea: Examine all subarrays: check if elements are unique using a set, and sum them to find the maximum erasure value.
steps: Iterate i from 0 to n - 1.
Maintain a HashSet of seen elements and a running sum.
For j from i to n - 1: if set contains nums[j] break; else add nums[j], update sum, update maxSum.
Return maxSum.
brute.whySlow: Scanning all subarrays and checking uniqueness takes O(n²) time.

optimal.idea: Sliding window with a HashSet and running sum: expand right, contract left on duplicate in O(n) time.
steps: Initialize Set<Integer> window = new HashSet<>(), left = 0, currentSum = 0, maxSum = 0.
For right from 0 to nums.length - 1: while window contains nums[right], remove nums[left], subtract nums[left] from currentSum, increment left.
Add nums[right] to window, add nums[right] to currentSum.
Update maxSum = max(maxSum, currentSum).
Return maxSum.

whyNext: Transforms the endpoint reduction problem from Minimum Size Subarray Sum (Seq 42) into finding the longest contiguous subarray whose sum equals totalSum - x using a sliding window.
hints: Removing elements from the ends that sum to x is equivalent to finding the longest middle subarray that sums to totalSum - x.
If target = totalSum - x is negative, return -1; if target == 0, return n.
Use sliding window to find longest subarray with sum == target. Result is n - maxLen.

brute.idea: Test all combinations of taking i elements from the left and j elements from the right that sum to x.
steps: Iterate i from 0 to n.
Iterate j from 0 to n - i.
If prefixSum[i] + suffixSum[j] == x, update minOps = min(minOps, i + j).
Return minOps if found, else -1.
brute.whySlow: Testing all prefix/suffix combinations takes O(n²) time.

optimal.idea: Find the maximum length of a subarray whose sum equals total - x using a linear sliding window.
steps: Compute target = sum(nums) - x. If target < 0 return -1. If target == 0 return nums.length.
Initialize l = 0, currentSum = 0, maxLen = -1.
For r from 0 to nums.length - 1: currentSum += nums[r].
While currentSum > target and l <= r: currentSum -= nums[l++].
If currentSum == target: maxLen = max(maxLen, r - l + 1).
Return maxLen == -1 ? -1 : nums.length - maxLen.

whyNext: Builds on sliding window cost bounds from Minimum Operations to Reduce X (Seq 341) by sorting elements and expanding a window where operations needed to match the rightmost element remain <= k.
hints: Sort the array: to maximize frequency, make a group of elements equal to the largest element in that group.
For a window [l, r], the operations needed to make all elements equal to nums[r] is (r - l + 1) * nums[r] - windowSum.

Sort nums. Initialize l = 0, windowSum = 0, maxFreq = 0. For r from 0 to n-1: windowSum += nums[r]. While (r - l + 1) * nums[r] - windowSum > k: windowSum -= nums[l++]; maxFreq = max(maxFreq, r - l + 1). Return maxFreq.

brute.idea: For every element nums[i], count how many other elements can be incremented to nums[i] using at most k operations.
steps: Sort nums.
For each index i from 0 to n - 1: initialize budget = k, freq = 1.
Iterate j from i - 1 down to 0: if budget >= nums[i] - nums[j], subtract cost and increment freq; else break.
Track maximum freq seen.
Return maximum freq.
brute.whySlow: Iterating backwards for every element takes O(n²) time.

optimal.idea: Sort array and use a sliding window to maintain (r - l + 1) * nums[r] - windowSum <= k in O(n log n) time.
steps: Sort nums ascending.
Initialize l = 0, long sum = 0, maxFreq = 0.
For r from 0 to nums.length - 1: add nums[r] to sum.
While (long)(r - l + 1) * nums[r] - sum > k: subtract nums[l++] from sum.
Update maxFreq = max(maxFreq, r - l + 1).
Return maxFreq.
